title: Apple Wallet Gets Long‑Awaited Feature in iOS 27, Boosting Convenience and Security
body:
Apple’s upcoming iOS 27 brings a long‑awaited capability to the Wallet app: users will finally be able to digitise physical tickets, boarding passes and loyalty cards by importing them directly into the system. The new “Import Physical Pass” function, announced alongside a suite of other Wallet enhancements, promises to streamline the way consumers manage everyday credentials, reducing reliance on paper and third‑party apps.

The feature works by allowing users to capture an image of a printed pass with their iPhone’s camera, after which the Wallet app analyses the visual data, extracts the relevant QR code or barcode, and creates a native pass that can be stored, refreshed and used just like any other digital ticket. Apple says the process is “secure, private and frictionless,” leveraging on‑device machine‑learning models to keep sensitive information out of the cloud. Once imported, the pass can be added to Apple Pay for quick access at the point of sale, and users can receive real‑time updates such as gate changes for flights or balance adjustments for loyalty programs.

The addition arrives at a time when digital wallets are becoming central to the mobile payments ecosystem. In 2023, Apple reported that more than 80 percent of iPhone users regularly use Wallet for at least one purpose, ranging from boarding passes to transit cards. Yet, despite the app’s broad adoption, many consumers still cling to physical documents because not every issuer provides a native digital version. By enabling a straightforward conversion from paper to digital, Apple is addressing a key pain point that has limited the Wallet’s universality. Industry analysts predict that the move could drive higher engagement rates, especially among frequent travelers and retail shoppers who juggle multiple loyalty cards.

Beyond the import tool, iOS 27 introduces several complementary upgrades. Users will see a refreshed interface that groups passes by category and highlights those that are about to expire, while a new “Smart Suggestions” panel recommends relevant passes based on location and time of day. The update also expands support for transit systems, adding contactless fare payment for additional cities worldwide and improving offline functionality for areas with spotty connectivity. For developers, Apple has released updated APIs that simplify the creation of dynamic passes, allowing real‑time data such as flight delays or event schedule changes to be pushed directly to a user’s Wallet without requiring a separate app.

The rollout could have broader implications for the competitive landscape of digital wallets. Google’s Wallet and Samsung’s Pass have already offered similar scanning capabilities, but Apple’s tight integration with iOS, its emphasis on privacy, and the sheer volume of its user base give it a strategic advantage. Moreover, the feature may nudge more merchants and service providers to adopt Apple’s PassKit standards, as the convenience of a universal import tool reduces the friction of onboarding new digital passes. Retailers that previously relied on proprietary QR‑code apps might find it more efficient to align with Apple’s ecosystem, potentially reshaping loyalty‑program strategies.

While the feature is poised to enhance user experience, privacy advocates will be watching how Apple handles the scanned data. The company assures that all image processing occurs locally on the device, but the ability to capture and store personal credentials could still raise concerns about misuse if a device is compromised. Apple’s longstanding stance on on‑device encryption and the requirement of Face ID or Touch ID to access Wallet should mitigate many risks, yet the conversation around data stewardship will likely continue as the functionality gains traction.

Looking ahead, the “Import Physical Pass” capability could serve as a stepping stone toward a fully paperless future. As more issuers recognize the demand for digital alternatives, the need for physical copies may dwindle, accelerating the adoption of contactless transactions and sustainable practices. With iOS 27 set to launch later this year, users and businesses alike will be watching to see how quickly the new Wallet features translate into everyday convenience and whether they spark a broader shift in how we store and present our most essential credentials.
